content.title: The Cotton Diplomacy Crisis — Foreign Intervention Question
content.description: British textile mills are starving for Southern cotton. The Confederacy withheld supplies, betting on British intervention. A decisive Confederate victory could sway Britain toward recognition.
content.source_notes: Use Confederate diplomatic correspondence, British cabinet and parliamentary debate summaries, cotton-market evidence, and historians of Civil War diplomacy before integration.
content.power_analysis: The branch should turn on British cabinet incentives, textile distress, Union counter-diplomacy, slavery policy, blockade risk, and whether Confederate battlefield success changes recognition calculations.
content.complexity_note: British commercial pressure did not automatically equal intervention; ministers had to weigh cotton, neutrality, anti-slavery politics, Union retaliation, and imperial risk.

choices.text: Push aggressively for immediate British recognition and intervention.
choices.costDescription: May alienate neutral parties, increases Union resolve
choices.consequence: Your aggressive diplomatic push in London gains sympathetic ears. British merchants pressure Parliament. The Ministry debates intervention. But Union counter-diplomacy is fierce. Britain remains officially neutral.

choices.text: Wait for more Confederate victories before requesting intervention.
choices.costDescription: Delays potential support, extends war timeline
choices.consequence: You counsel patience. After Antietam, Northern success seems assured to the British. Recognition never comes. The Confederacy fights on alone. Your strategy preserves future options.

comments: Reviewed and approved for future branch work, not current spine insertion.
review_note: Approved as a future divergence-only branch candidate. It should attach to Potomac leverage / Antietam rather than become a disconnected standalone turn.

content.title: Kentucky's Neutrality — A House Divided
content.description: Kentucky is the border state everyone wants. Governor Magoffin desperately wants neutrality, but both governments covet the state. Military movements could shatter neutrality.
content.source_notes: Use 1861 Kentucky neutrality proclamations, Lincoln administration correspondence, Magoffin's public statements, and military records around Columbus, Louisville, and the Ohio River corridor.
content.power_analysis: The branch should turn on river control, state neutrality, Unionist and secessionist blocs, rail access, recruitment, and the danger that premature occupation changes Kentucky's alignment.
content.complexity_note: Neutrality was not simple sympathy for either side; it was a political bargain inside a divided border state whose military geography both governments needed.

choices.text: Respect Kentucky's neutrality, move supplies quietly.
choices.consequence: You respect Kentucky's declared neutrality. Union supplies flow quietly through neutral corridors. But Confederate sympathizers infiltrate the state apparatus. Kentucky slides toward secession.

choices.text: Move the Army in to secure Louisville and strategic points.
choices.costDescription: Alienates Kentucky, may drive it toward Confederacy
choices.consequence: Union troops occupy Louisville and key river points. Kentucky explodes in anger. Secessionists rally. But Union control prevents Confederate invasion. Kentucky remains contested but Union-held.

comments: Reviewed and approved for future branch work, not current spine insertion.
review_note: Approved as a future early-war branch candidate. It should attach to the opening border-state sequence rather than expand the current spine immediately.
